Does Safely Ejecting From a USB Port Actually Do Anything?
Yes. It insures that any cached files that have yet to be written, get written. If the file directory structure gets damaged by incomplete writes, you will lose access to all data on that drive.
Also it'll stop new requests from being added to the queue.
Makes sense.. I guess I could make sure that all programs have stopped reading/writing to a drive and just yank it, but it's probably better not to.

In fact you don't know when a program stopped reading or writting on your media. There are caching mechanisms for IO performances that makes writes in Ram instead on the media. Then at regular intervals the media write.

I had an old "Virgin" brand MP3 player that I couldn't get to work for the life of me. Until one day I didn't safely remove and found all the files present and accounted for on the player. I still don't understand how that could work. Maybe material for an ELI5 one day! (unless someone can now of course)
A horribly broken filesystem implementation in the firmware is all I can think of.

Yes.

When you write to a drive there is a technology called write back. The system kernel caches the write request, and based upon the specifics of your kernel build, may not actually write to the underlying media until the cache is directed to flush. Again, depending upon the kernel tune, this cache-flush could be initiated when the cache fills or performed on a timed basis. This helps to speed up whatever you are actively doing as the application doesn't have to wait for the directed write operation to report back as being successfully written to the thumb drive. The application can just keep on chugging along, all the while sending write requests that are being placed into a waiting queue, and the user doesn't have to experience any sluggish perfomance. When you direct the OS to eject the key, the kernel will flush all of the write buffers/cache and ensure that anything still waiting to be written to disk is actually written to disk.

Now, while some operating systems such as Windows supposedly have this performance-enhancing option disabled by default for USB drives, it's no guarantee that it's actually working as advertised. Just hit the eject button, and leave the praying for jihadist suicide bombers.
